cards.title: The first program
cards.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, including a method for computing Bernoulli numbers — often called the first computer program.

cards.title: The moth in the machine
cards.text: In 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II taped a moth into the logbook as the “first actual case of bug being found”. Engineers had already been calling faults bugs for decades.

cards.title: ENIAC
cards.text: ENIAC, completed in 1945, used about 18,000 vacuum tubes, weighed around 27 tonnes and filled a large room.

cards.title: “LO”
cards.text: The first message over ARPANET, in October 1969, was meant to be “LOGIN”. The system crashed after two letters, so the first message was “LO”.

cards.title: The Web's birthplace
cards.text: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989, and the first website went online in 1991.

cards.title: Moore's law
cards.text: In 1965 Gordon Moore noted that the number of components on a chip was doubling every year; in 1975 he revised it to roughly every two years.

cards.question: Whose 1936 paper on computable numbers laid the foundations of theoretical computer science?
Which company released the first commercial microprocessor, the 4004, in 1971?
Which language did Dennis Ritchie create at Bell Labs in the early 1970s?
Who created the Python programming language?
What does GNU stand for?
cards.explanation: A recursive acronym, chosen by Richard Stallman in 1983.

cards.question: Claude Shannon's 1948 paper “A Mathematical Theory of Communication” founded which field?

cards.statement: The word “bug” was invented when a moth was found inside a computer.
cards.explanation: Thomas Edison was already describing technical faults as bugs in the 1870s; the 1947 moth was a joke on an existing term.

cards.statement: Bill Gates said “640K ought to be enough for anybody.”
cards.explanation: There's no evidence he ever said it, and he has denied it.

cards.statement: The Apollo Guidance Computer that flew to the Moon had about 4 KB of RAM.
cards.explanation: It had 2,048 words of erasable memory (roughly 4 KB) and about 72 KB of read-only rope memory.

cards.statement: The World Wide Web and the Internet are the same thing.
cards.explanation: The Internet is the global network; the Web is one service running on it, alongside email, streaming and more.
